## Abstract

BACKGROUND: Personal care products (PCPs) contain endocrine-disrupting chemicals

(EDCs) linked to hormonally-sensitive diseases. Population studies have found associations

between prenatal EDC exposure and childhood asthma; however, few have investigated adult-

onset asthma.

OBJECTIVES: We investigated the associations between commonly used PCPs and the risk of

adult-onset asthma in a prospective cohort study of U.S. women.

METHODS: We analyzed 39,408 participants from the Sister Study (2003-2009). The

participants self-reported their usage frequency of 41 PCPs in the 12-month period before

baseline. Latent classes were used to identify groups with similar usage patterns (‘infrequent’,

‘moderate’, ‘frequent’) within types of products (‘beauty’, ‘everyday hair’, ‘hygiene’, and

‘skincare’). Multivariable Cox regression models were used to assess the associations between

PCP use and incident adult-onset asthma.

RESULTS: Over an average 12.5-year follow-up, 1,774 incident asthma cases were identified.

Compared to infrequent users, moderate (hazard ratio [HR]=1.21 (95% confidence interval

(CI):1.07,1.37)) and frequent (HR=1.22 (95%CI:1.08,1.38)) users of beauty products had

significantly higher asthma risk. Similar associations were observed for hygiene (moderate:

HR=1.14 (95%CI:1.01,1.29) and frequent: HR=1.20 (95%CI:1.06,1.36)) and skincare products

(moderate: HR=1.21 (95%CI:1.06,1.38) and frequent: HR=1.20 (95%CI:1.06,1.35)). Several

individual everyday hair products (hair spray, hair styling gel/mousse, and pomade or hair grease)

were positively associated with asthma risk, but associations were not detected for everyday hair

latent classes.

Introduction 1

2

Personal care products (PCPs) contain complex mixtures of endocrine-disrupting chemicals 3

(EDCs) including per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), parabens, phthalates, phenols 1-3, 4

as well as other hazardous components. Chronic exposure to EDCs has been facilitated by the 5

widespread use of PCPs in the daily lives of the general population 4. The patterns of PCP use 6

differ by subgroups defined by sex 5, race/ethnicity 3,6, and age 7. In particular, women have been 7

found to use disproportionately more PCPs compared to men and may be at higher risk of 8

adverse health consequences of exposure. EDCs found in PCPs have been linked to hormonally- 9

sensitive chronic diseases, including cardiovascular diseases as well as breast and ovarian cancer 10

among women 8,9. 11

In the United States (U.S.), asthma is one of the most common chronic, non-communicable 12

respiratory diseases, affecting over 27 million people 10,11 and the prevalence among adults 13

increased from 6.9% in 2001 to 8.0% in 2021 12. Asthma is more common among adult women 14

(10.8%) than men (6.5%); however, the underlying reasons are unclear 13. Recently, there has 15

been growing concern about the impact of environmental chemicals on asthma development. 16

Asthma is a hormonally-response disease 14-16 and population studies have reported potential 17

associations with exposure to EDCs in PCPs 17,18. However, most of the current literature focuses 18

on the risk of childhood asthma, while few epidemiological studies have investigated the 19

association between exposure to EDCs and the risk of adult-onset asthma. 20

To address the gaps in knowledge, we investigated the associations between PCP use and risk of 21

incident adult-onset asthma among U.S. women from the Sister Study. To better capture the risks 22

associated with the simultaneous use of multiple products in real-world settings, we investigated 23

Methods 28

29

Study design and population 30

31

The Sister Study is a prospective cohort study that enrolled 50,884 women residing in U.S. and 32

Puerto Rico from 2003 to 2009 19. Women were eligible for the Sister Study if they were 35-74 33

years of age, had at least one sister diagnosed with breast cancer, and never had a diagnosis of 34

ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) or invasive breast cancer. Women completed a computer- 35

assisted telephone interview and self-administered questionnaires at enrollment to assess 36

demographics (e.g., age, race/ethnicity, educational attainment, and household income), 37

reproductive and medical history (e.g., menopausal status and family history of asthma), and 38

lifestyle factors (e.g., smoking status, alcohol consumption, and recreational physical activity). 39

Height and weight were measured by a trained examiner during a home visit at baseline and used 40

to determine body mass index (BMI, kg/m2). Detailed information on data collection and 41

questionnaires can be found on the Sister Study website 20. 42

Among the 50,884 women, we excluded those who were diagnosed with prevalent asthma prior 43

to baseline (n=7,179), diagnosed at unknown timing relative to the completion of all baseline 44

study components (n=1,613), had uncertain asthma diagnoses (n=5), or withdrew from the study 45

(n=5). We also excluded women who did not complete the PCP questionnaire module (n=2,674). 46

Personal care product use 54

55

The participants self-reported their frequency of use of 41 PCPs in the 12-month period before 56

baseline. The frequency of use for each PCP included: 1) did not use, 2) used less than once a 57

month, 3) used 1-3 times per month, 4) used 1-5 times per week, 5) used more than 5 times per 58

week. To identify latent classes of PCP use, the 41 PCPs were grouped into twelve beauty 59

products (PCPs listed in Table S3), seven everyday hair products (PCPs listed in Table S4), eight 60

hygiene products (PCPs listed in Table S5), and fourteen skincare products (PCPs listed in Table 61

S6) based on a priori knowledge and correlation structure 9. 62

65

Participants were contacted for either annual health update forms or detailed follow-up 66

questionnaires, which included health updates on new doctor’s diagnosis of asthma. Participants 67

who reported a diagnosis of asthma during the follow-up were defined as incident cases 68

(n=1,774). Among asthma cases, 98.5% self-reported a diagnosis of unspecified asthma 69

Statistical analysis 74

75

The distribution of the participants’ baseline characteristics was presented by adult-onset asthma. 76

We used Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients to estimate pairwise correlations for frequency 77

of  use for 41 PCPs. 78

Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to estimate hazard ratios 79

(HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the associations between individual PCPs and the 80

adult-onset asthma risk. Consistent with previous studies, we accounted for age as the timescale 81

in the Cox models 9,21. Further, we adjusted for race/ethnicity (African American/Black, 82

Hispanic/Latina non-Black, non-Hispanic White, other, or missing), educational attainment (high 83

school or less, some college, college and above, or missing), annual household income 84

(<$50,000, $50,000-<$100,000, ≥$100,000, or missing), menopausal status at enrollment 85

(premenopausal, postmenopausal, or missing), smoking status (never, past, current, or missing), 86

secondhand smoke exposure (continuous, years), alcohol consumption (never or past, current <1 87

drink, current ≥1 drinks, or missing), and BMI (continuous, kg/m2). 88

We used PROC LCA in SAS statistical software (version 9.4; SAS Institute Inc.) to conduct 89

latent class analysis (LCA) to identify groups of individuals with similar patterns of PCP use 22. 90

Use of Individual Products and Incident Adult-onset Asthma 160

161

Among the 12 individual beauty products, frequent users of blush or rouge (P-trend<0.01), 162

lipstick (P-trend=0.01), artificial nails or fill-ins (P-trend=0.03), and cuticle cream (P- 163

trend<0.01) had higher risk of asthma compared with non-users (Table S3). A higher risk of 164

asthma was observed in the group that used eye liner, eye shadow, or foundation makeup 165

compared to non-users, but the trend was non-monotonic. For the individual everyday hair 166

products, frequent users of pomade or hair grease had increased risk of asthma compared with 167

non-users (P-trend<0.01). The groups that used hair spray or hair styling gel/mousse 1-5 times 168

per week had a higher risk of asthma than the non-users, but the trend was non-monotonic (Table 169

S4). Among the hygiene products, only talcum powder use on the vaginal area had a significant 170

positive association with asthma risk (P-trend=0.02, Table S5). Among the 14 individual 171

skincare products, anti-aging/wrinkle products use and age spot lightener use was positively 172

associated with asthma risk (P-trend<0.01). Compared to non-users, increased risks of asthma 173

were found in the groups who used blemish/acne products, cleansing cream, facial masks, or 174

self-tanning products, but the trends were not monotonic (Table S6). 175

In this large prospective cohort study with detailed information on use of PCPs, we found that 179

frequent use of beauty, hygiene, and skincare products was associated with increased risk of 180

adult-onset asthma among U.S. women. Several individual everyday hair products were 181

positively associated with adult-onset asthma risk, but the latent classes for everyday hair 182

products were not. To our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate the relationships of 183

commonly used individual and complex mixtures of PCPs with future risk of adult-onset asthma. 184

185

Previous epidemiologic studies that investigated the impact of exposure to EDCs on the risk of 186

asthma have primarily focused on the association between prenatal exposure to EDCs and their 187

children's risk of childhood asthma. Data from a Danish cohort of 738 pregnant women and their 188

children showed that higher maternal perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoate 189

(PFOA) exposure during pregnancy was associated with increased risk of non-atopic asthma 190

phenotype by age 6 years 24. Berger et al. measured urinary concentration of the 10 PCP 191

biomarkers (three phthalate metabolites, three parabens, and four other phenols), and suggested 192

that prenatal urinary concentration of triclosan was associated with increased odds of probable 193

asthma in their children, especially in girls 25. Prenatal urinary metabolites of short-chain 194

phthalates such as butylbenzyl phthalate (BBzP) and di-n-butyl phthalate (DnBP) were found to 195

be positively associated with a history of asthma-like symptoms and the diagnosis of current 196

asthma in children 26. Data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 197

(NHANES) 2005–2006 showed that higher urinary monobenzyl phthalate (MBzP) concentration 198

was associated with current asthma and allergic symptoms in adults but not in children 27. 199

However, there are few prospective cohort studies on adult-onset asthma risk, and most 200

investigations assessed single EDC at a time. Using one spot serum or urine biomarker 201

204

Several studies have suggested that the differences in the use of PCPs may contribute to the 205

racial/ethnic disparities in asthma risk 29. Hair products and feminine hygiene products used by 206

Black women contained multiple chemicals associated with asthma, and higher levels of paraben 207

and diethyl phthalate (DEP) were observed in biomonitoring samples from Black women 208

compared with non-Hispanic White women 29-31. In our study, the frequency of beauty, hygiene, 209

and skincare product use were positively associated with asthma risk in non-Hispanic White 210

women. Stronger association between the frequent use of hygiene products and increased risk of 211

asthma was observed in Black, Hispanic, and other minority groups, but this association did not 212

reach statistical significance, which may be due to the small sample size and case number. 213

Similar association was observed for everyday hair products in Black women. As such, large- 214

scale prospective epidemiological studies with diverse populations are needed to determine the 215

impact of PCP use on racial/ethnic disparities in asthma risk. 216

217

We used self-reported asthma status in this study, which was previously found to be valid in 218

North America and Europe when compared to medical records 32-36. In particular, a study 219

0.52–0.63) to 0.67 (95% CI: 0.62–0.72) 36. Furthermore, a previous study conducted among 222

European populations found good agreement between self-reported and registered age at adult- 223

onset asthma among patients 37. 224

Our finding suggested that EDCs potentially have a greater impact on the respiratory health of 226

postmenopausal women. In support of this finding, it has been reported that phthalate 227

metabolites are associated with differences in the concentrations of sex hormones that regulate 228

many autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, including asthma, only in postmenopausal women 229

38. Additionally, the duration of exposure may be important because older women may have had 230

greater cumulative exposure to EDCs over their lifetime. However, we cannot discount the 231

possibility that the non-significant association found among younger premenopausal women was 232

due to limited sample size, as the average age at enrollment was age 55 years. 233

234

Understanding the biological pathways through which EDCs may increase the risk of asthma is 235

important for understanding disease pathogenesis. Sex hormones play a key role in asthma 236

pathogenesis 39, and the sex hormone-disrupting effects of EDCs may affect the risk of adult- 237

onset asthma 40. Various phenotypes of adult onset asthma have been described in adulthood; one 238

for example in older women is associated with obesity, more symptoms, lack of T helper 2 cell 239

(Th2) markers, and less response to steroids 41. Endocrine influences may have particularly 240

contributed to this phenotype 42. A direct effect of EDC exposure is suppression of inflammatory 241

processes, which may lead to insufficient immune responses against bacteria, fungi, and viruses. 242

Previous studies have shown that a skewed balance in Th1 / Th2 can predispose children to the 243

development of asthma 43. Animal studies also showed that allergic asthmatic mice exposed to 244

EDC had a significant increase in inflammatory cell infiltration. Triclosan has been shown to 245

stimulate non-type 2 pro-inflammatory cytokines from immune cells, and these may be potential 246

mediators of the late-onset, non-allergic asthma phenotype 44. Exposure to EDCs may also 247

254

Our study had numerous strengths. First, our study had a large sample size and the prospective 255

study design minimizes recall bias and reverse causation. Second, we leveraged comprehensive 256

questionnaire data on exposure to various PCPs relevant to female U.S. populations. Here, we 257

investigated the impact of complex mixtures of PCPs, which better reflects exposure profiles in 258

real-world settings. This is important considering that exposure to multiple EDCs can result in 259

synergistic, antagonistic, or cumulative effects (for compounds acting via similar pathways). 260

Further, there is substantial toxicological evidence that mixtures are more toxic than the 261

individual compounds 48. 262

263

Our investigation had some limitations. First, the impact of specific EDCs could not be 264

investigated due to lack of information on product ingredients or brands. However, self-reported 265

product use may reflect exposures to complex mixtures of chemicals, which may be 266

contaminants or derivatives produced during manufacturing or storage, or may not be stated on 267

the label by manufacturers.9 Second, we did not have information on duration of PCP use. Since 268

women tend to use PCPs long-term as part of their daily or monthly routine, our findings likely 269

reflect the effects of chronic exposure to PCPs. Further epidemiological data are needed to 270

self-reported asthma status, the use of self-reported asthma status does not reflect the 273

Gender differences have been reported in the outcomes of xenoestrogen-induced asthma 49,50. 278

health outcomes related to EDC exposure. Lastly, the analyses for Black and other minority 281

women were underpowered; therefore, further replication in diverse populations is warranted. 282

283

The current regulations for personal care products have several limitations. The U.S, Food and 284

Drug Administration (FDA) requires that cosmetics and personal care products be safe for 285

consumers when used as intended, and do not contain prohibited ingredients. However, except 286

for color additives, the FDA does not require premarket approval for cosmetics, and cosmetic 287

companies are responsible for substantiating the safety of their products and ingredients prior to 288

marketing. In addition, manufacturers are not required by FDA to register, file ingredient 289

information, or report adverse reactions.51 The Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act of 290

2022 is the most significant expansion of the FDA's cosmetics regulatory jurisdiction since the 291

Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938. PCPs that are not considered cosmetics are 292

regulated variably depending on their intended use. Our findings highlight the need for 293
